Commentary.Commentary: We are back. We have 18 overs left in the day. The umpires are out in the middle. South African players are seen in a huddle near the ropes before taking the field. Takudzwanashe Kaitano and Prince Masvaure are the two openers for Zimbabwe. Codi Yusuf has the new cherry in hand. Let's play...
... FOURTH INNINGS ...

For Zimbabwe, the absence of Blessing Muzarabani was sorely felt. The lanky pacer was only eligible to bowl late in the second session after missing most of the first due to illness. Wellington Masakadza picked up 4 wickets while Tanaka Chivanga and Vincent Masekesa each picked up 2  wickets and Blessing chipped in with one on his return. Zimbabwe now face a herculean task, with their immediate focus being to get through the remaining passage of play today with as little damage as possible. Back in a bit for Zimbabwe's reply.

Mulder's partnership with Kyle Verreynne added significant value, as the pair stitched together a 104-run stand. Although both eventually departed, Corbin Bosch and captain Keshav Maharaj took over, scoring at a brisk pace to extend the lead further. Both Bosch and Maharaj fell but the Proteas continued to bat before eventually being bowled out for 369.

South Africa end with a mammoth lead of 536, bringing an end to a long and tiring stint in the field for Zimbabwe. The Proteas built on their first-innings lead of 167, continuing their dominance over the hosts. While Matthew Breetzke couldn't get going, Tony de Zorzi and David Bedingham made decent contributions. However, it was Wiaan Mulder who stole the show with a magnificent 147, anchoring the innings and setting the stage for a substantial lead.

... DAY 3, SESSION 2 ...

South Africa might want to add another 100 runs before making a call on the declaration. It was the spinners who had a major say in the morning session, and while not every ball is turning square just yet, conditions are expected to become more challenging as the Test progresses. As for Zimbabwe, it will be about hanging in and trying to bowl with greater control, something they lacked in the first couple of hours. Do join us again shortly for the second session.

Wiaan Mulder and David Bedingham kept the scoreboard ticking, and as the partnership grew, many were left wondering where the next wicket would come from for Zimbabwe. But just when things looked flat for the hosts, they roared back with three quick wickets. Vincent Masekesa claimed two of them, richly deserving the rewards for his persistence and the control he showed throughout the morning. Despite that flurry of wickets, Zimbabwe failed to build sustained pressure for the rest of the session, not even on Mulder, who was closing in on his century and eventually reached the milestone in the final over before the break.

SESSION SUMMARY - 30 overs, 136 runs and 4 wickets. A session that reflects the overall state of the Test. Zimbabwe managed to pick up wickets, but South Africa kept the scoreboard moving at a healthy rate of 4.53 runs per over and have now stretched their lead to 352 runs. Tanaka Chivanga once again bowled his heart out in the session and managed to strike early, but he lacked support from the other end. His usual partner in crime, Blessing Muzarabani, was off the field for over an hour and a half, which significantly hampered the bowling resources available to Craig Ervine during that stretch.

PITCH REPORT - Ed Rainsford is near the deck. Informs that it’s noticeably colder this morning, which could play a role in the field, especially when it comes to catching. Mentions that from a bowling perspective, there was steep bounce from one particular end when Zimbabwe were batting yesterday, and the seamers will be eyeing that area once again today. Shaun Pollock has a closer look at that area. Observes that there's a really good grass covering, but also a major divot which Codi Yusuf targeted from around the wicket. States that when the ball lands on the edge of those divots, it can take off steeply, and as a batter, there’s not much you can do.

South Africa's Wiaan Mulder is also in for a flash interview. Mulder says that it was really simple for him to try and hit the top of off and mix it up with the odd bouncer. Shares that there was some steep bounce from the pitch and that hit the splice of the bat.  Adds that sometimes it keeps so low that LBW comes into the picture. Mentions that when you have Marco Jansen, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi who have express pace, his job gets easy as he doesn't try to do anything different. Observes that from one end, there was a bit more bounce and live grass from where the pacers got more purchase. States that batting at number 3 is tricky and it is something he has not done a lot in domestic cricket. Adds that in his school days, he used to bowl 10 overs and bat at number 3 in the second innings. Observes that in International cricket it's different, but he's a fit guy, but he's now focusing more on the mental side and whenever he gets some time in the middle, he tries to close his eyes and try to focus as much as he can. Concludes that the surface has not changed much, as facing Blessing Muzarabani was a bit tricky and he bowled really well in the second innings as compared to the first. Further says that Blessing also got some extra bounce with his height.

Sean Williams is in for a chat. He says that they, as a team, have prepared well for the series. He adds that he has prepared for Keshav Maharaj and the left-arm seamers. Mentions that the pitch is good but it is a bit challenging for left-handers due to a patch around the off stump. He ends by saying that he is trying to be brave and lead as an example for the younger guys.

As we look ahead to Day 3, Zimbabwean bowlers will be looking to make the most of the conditions to strike early in the morning session. But on the flip side, South Africa, who hold firm control on this Test, will be looking to put up a mammoth target on the board. Either way, the moving day of this Test is about to unfold. Settle in, as the first ball of Day 3 is just around the corner.

On Day 2, after South Africa declared their first innings at 418/9, Zimbabwe's batting faced an early onslaught from debutant Codi Yusuf, who took two quick wickets, compounded by opener Brian Bennett retiring hurt with a concussion from a Kwena Maphaka delivery. Despite this, Sean Williams and Craig Ervine mounted a resilient partnership, though Ervine was eventually stumped by Keshav Maharaj. Williams continued to defy the Proteas' disciplined bowling, reaching his sixth Test hundred, but eventually Zimbabwe were bundled over for 251, handing the tourists a 167-run lead. After the early loss of Matthew Breetzke. Tony de Zorzi and Wiaan Mulder steadied the ship with their solid batting, ending the day at 49/1, extending the lead to 216 runs.

Hello and welcome from Bulawayo! Here we are for the 'Moving Day' of this opening Test with South Africa firmly in the ascendancy. The Proteas will be eyeing a commanding position to put the game out of Zimbabwe’s reach, while for the hosts, it’s all about digging deep and staying in the contest.
... DAY 3, SESSION 1 ...

Well then, another gripping day of Test cricket has zipped by. As we roll into the all-important Day 3, the classic ‘Moving Day’, South Africa will look to steady the ship early, aiming for a solid first session to lay the groundwork for a commanding lead. Zimbabwe, meanwhile, will be fired up to strike hard in that probing first hour and keep the visitors within reach. The first ball is set to be delivered at 8 am GMT on Monday, 30th June, but don’t miss the buildup and join us an hour earlier for all the exciting analysis. Cheers.

Armed with a handy 167-run cushion, South Africa’s second innings began on a shaky note, losing a wicket within the opening two overs. This time, Zimbabwe unleashed their pacers right away, an approach they’d held back from in the first innings. Tanaka Chivanga kept his rhythm going by removing Breetzke early, while Muzarabani applied pressure with tight lines and smart lengths, making scoring tricky under the fading light. There were a few nervous moments with edges beaten and tempers tested, but de Zorzi and Mulder dug in and saw it through with an unbeaten 48-run stand before the day ended due to bad light.

Sean Williams carried on the fight into the final session, holding firm even as wickets kept tumbling around him. Vincent Masakesa showed solid defensive technique and offered valuable support during a gritty stand. But nearly an hour into the session, Keshav Maharaj returned to break through, removing Williams for a well-crafted 137. That wicket left Zimbabwe teetering at 249 for 8, and with the tail exposed, it took South Africa just 15 more deliveries to polish off the innings. Wiaan Mulder came up trumps with a four-for, while Codi Yusuf and Keshav Maharaj shared the spoils as well with three wickets apiece.

However, as one brings two, Zimbabwe suffered a setback, collapsing from 167 for 3 to 201 for 6. The dismissal of Craig Ervine exposed a vulnerable lower middle order, and South Africa seized the moment to pile on the pressure. Despite the flurry of wickets, Zimbabwe still managed to chalk up 118 runs in the afternoon session, thanks largely to Sean Williams’ composed innings. The veteran brought up his sixth Test century, doing his every bit to narrow the deficit. There were nervy moments too, especially with Codi Yusuf consistently beating the outside edge with that steep bounce and deviation.

With the ball getting soft and old, and the second session offering good batting conditions, both the vastly experienced batters made hay in the sun. But Keshav Maharaj stepped in with a beauty of a delivery to break the 91-run stand for the third wicket. One good thing for Zimbabwe was that they didn't go into a shell after that, as Sean Williams, with his calming presence, and Wessly Medhevere counterattacked on anything loose thrown at them. Keshav Maharaj did get a good grip and bite in the second session, tripled with extra bounce, but the batters did take him on as well.

South Africa’s overnight declaration at 418/9 set the tone for a brisk Day 2. Under sunny skies and chilly conditions, the pace attack had early joy. Kwena Maphaka, though, battled some rust, but debutant Codi Yusuf struck twice in his first spell with probing lengths that skidded off the deck. Zimbabwe’s lead-up was further disrupted when Brian Bennett left the field after a scary blow to the helmet, eventually being diagnosed with a late concussion. Mulder and Bosch countered with disciplined lines, yet it was Yusuf’s second stint, harping the ball up from that ideal six-to-eight-metre window, that really tested the Chevrons’ technique.

South Africa can walk off with a sense of control after a productive Day 2, having edged the day with two sessions to their name. They struck early in the morning with clinical precision, before Zimbabwe rallied back through Williams and Ervine to make the afternoon theirs. But just when the tide looked like turning, the Proteas stormed back late in the day with a flurry of wickets, tilting the session count 2-1 in their favour. What’s added even more intrigue is the brisk tempo this Test has taken on. Runs have flowed, wickets have tumbled, and the match has advanced at a gallop.
